title: The Portrait of a Lady (Prose, Hornbill)
tagline: Khushwant Singh’s portrait of his grandmother: companionship in the village, distance in the city, and a silent farewell.

overview.intro: The opening prose of Hornbill is a portrait drawn without a single anecdote of great events: an old woman, a rosary, a pair of sparrows. Khushwant Singh recalls his grandmother as she was across three settings — the village, the city, and the years abroad — and in each the relationship changes while the woman does not. The unit studies how the narrative moves through those three settings, how humour and affection coexist, and how the final scene with the sparrows completes the portrait the title promises.

facts.label: Author

facts.label: The grandmother

learningOutcomes: Trace the change in the grandmother’s life across the village, city and abroad.
Explain the contrast between the two schools and what the grandmother made of them.
Account for the significance of the sparrows in the final scene.
Identify the narrative voice: affection, humour and restraint.
Answer extract and short answer questions on the text with textual support.

blocks.text: The portrait begins in the village, where the grandmother is the centre of a small world. She is old and wrinkled, spends her day spinning the rosary and telling her beads, and is rendered beautiful in the narrator’s memory rather than young in fact. Her morning routine binds her to her grandson: she wakes him, washes and dresses him, eats breakfast with him, and walks with him to the school, which in those days was held in a temple attached to the house. The walk home repeats the pattern with the village dogs, whom they feed on the way — a detail that establishes her generosity as instinctive rather than performed.

The school itself matters for what it lacks. It was a temple school, so the children were taught the holy scriptures and the grandmother sat inside with the other women while the lessons happened. She was happy with a schooling that mixed learning with devotion, because it meant her grandson’s day and her day followed the same rhythm. Everything in this section is arranged around togetherness: the same path, the same hours, the same food, the same prayers. The later separations are measured against it.

blocks.caption: The village pattern of the day
rows: She wakes, washes and dresses him; breakfast together
She walks him to the temple school and sits inside
They walk home, feeding the village dogs on the way
Rosary and beads; the same room, the same companions

learn.title: The city years: the schools and the distance

blocks.text: The move to the city changes the shape of everything. The grandmother can no longer accompany him to school: he goes by bus to an English school, which means her day and his day now run on separate tracks. She objects to the content of what he learns — English, science, music, and above all no religion — and the music lesson becomes the point on which she turns hardest, since to her ear the teaching of song to a boy is something like its corruption. The narrator reports her displeasure without defending himself, and the comedy of the passage is gentle rather than mocking: a grandmother’s bewilderment at a curriculum.

At university the distance widens from disagreement to indifference. She can no longer follow his studies, so she stops trying, and takes to feeding the sparrows in the courtyard. The relationship that was once constant contact becomes, in the city, two people living parallel lives in the same house. When he goes abroad for five years she sees him off without ceremony, and he records her as sitting by the window, telling her beads, rather than as grieving — which is both a restraint in the telling and the point of the portrait: her devotion did not depend on his presence.

items: The grandmother loses her place in his day when he travels to school by bus.
She is unhappy about the absence of religious teaching and about the music lessons.
At university they share almost nothing, and she turns to feeding sparrows.
The five years abroad pass with no dramatic display of feeling on either side.
Distance is shown through routine rather than stated through commentary.

learn.title: The return, the illness and the sparrows

blocks.text: He comes home after five years and finds that she has aged but not changed: she welcomes him, and that evening takes her turn to celebrate by singing and beating a drum, an act that reunites the old companions for one night. The next day she falls ill, and the illness is treated as the natural close rather than as a crisis — she is not sent for a doctor in the narrator’s telling, she prays, and she dies, with the family assembling around her bed. The narrator has already told us that she had been waiting for her last hour, so the death arrives as fulfilment rather than shock.

The closing scene is the one the portrait is remembered for. Sparrows gather in the courtyard and by her body, silent — no chirping, no fluttering — and they refuse the bread scattered for them. Silence at a funeral is ordinary; silence from sparrows is not, and the refusal of food completes the impression that the household has lost its centre. The narrator says they mourned like us, and the sentence quietly transfers the grandmother’s own companionship to the birds she had fed for years. The portrait ends where portraits should: with an image that summarises a life without comment.

blocks.caption: The three settings and what each takes from the relationship
rows: All day together, temple school, the dogs
Five years apart, one evening of celebration
Illness, death, and the sparrows’ silence

learn.title: Narrative voice and how the portrait is made

blocks.text: The piece is told in the past tense by an adult looking back, and its voice is its achievement. The humour is affectionate and self-deprecating: the narrator mocks his own youthful impatience as much as his grandmother’s bewilderment, and he never argues with her. Restraint is equally deliberate — he withholds grief, states the death in a sentence, and lets the sparrows carry the feeling. That technique, of stating little and arranging much, is what turns a family memory into a portrait.

For examination purposes the story asks for evidence rather than admiration. Short answers should quote or closely paraphrase one detail from the village, the city and the ending, since the question will ask for change over time. Longer answers should treat the grandmother as a figure of continuity in a changing world: her routines do not alter while his education, language and geography do, and the sparrows are the final proof that her world of attachment continued independently of him.

items.text: Feeding the village dogs on the walk home.
items.note: Establishes her generosity as routine and unselfconscious before any later scene depends on it.
A non-human response that carries the grief the narrator refuses to state.

keyPoints: The grandmother is unnamed; the portrait is of a type as much as a person.
In the village she accompanies the narrator to the temple school.
She feeds the village dogs on the walk home each day.
The move to the city separates their days because he travels by bus.
She objects to the absence of religion and to the music lessons.
At university she feeds sparrows in the courtyard.
He is away for five years; she sees him off without display.
On his return she sings and beats a drum that evening.
She dies the next day after praying, without drama in the telling.
The sparrows gather silent and refuse bread, completing the portrait.

Humour and affection run together — quote the narrator’s self-mockery where you can.
Short answers: name the change, then cite the routine that shows it.

questions.prompt: In the village, the narrator and his grandmother went to a school held in:
options: A temple attached to the house
questions.answer: A temple attached to the house
questions.explanation: The temple school is why she could sit inside while he was taught, which shaped the togetherness of the village years.

questions.prompt: After the move to the city, the grandmother was most unhappy about:
options: The absence of religion and the music lessons
questions.answer: The absence of religion and the music lessons
questions.explanation: She could accept English and science, but no religion and the teaching of music to her grandson offended her sense of schooling.

questions.prompt: During the years at university the grandmother occupied herself by:
questions.explanation: With no shared activity left, feeding the sparrows became her daily companionship.

questions.prompt: The sparrows at the end of the story function chiefly as:
options: A symbol of the grandmother’s continuing world of attachment
Evidence that the household had neglected her
A sign of the village setting returning
questions.answer: A symbol of the grandmother’s continuing world of attachment
questions.explanation: They were her daily companions in life and their silence mourns with the family, transferring the attachment the narrator will not state himself.

questions.prompt: The narrator was away from home for ________ years while studying abroad.
questions.explanation: He returns after five years to find that she has aged but her habits are unchanged.

questions.prompt: On the evening of his return, the grandmother celebrated by singing and beating a ________ .
questions.explanation: The celebration reunites the old companions for one evening before her illness.

questions.prompt: Describe the grandmother’s routine in the village.
questions.answer: In the village her day was built around her grandson: she woke him, washed and dressed him, and ate breakfast with him; she walked with him to the temple school and sat inside with the other women while the lessons went on; and they walked home together, feeding the village dogs on the way. The rest of her day was spent spinning the rosary and telling her beads. The routine matters because every part of it is shared, which is what the later city years will take away.
questions.explanation: The answer must show the sharing of each activity rather than list her habits alone.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator show the growing distance between himself and his grandmother?
questions.answer: The distance is shown through changes in routine rather than stated as a feeling. In the city he travels to an English school by bus, so their days no longer coincide, and she is distressed by a curriculum that contains no religion and includes music lessons, which she considers improper for a boy. At university the separation deepens into indifference: he can no longer explain what he studies, she stops trying to understand, and she takes to feeding the sparrows in the courtyard while he reads alone. When he goes abroad for five years she sees him off without any display of grief, and he reports her as sitting by the window telling her beads. The narrator never says they grew apart; he lets the timetable, the objections and the separate occupations say it.
questions.explanation: Three stages must be given with the concrete detail that shows each, and the method — showing rather than telling — noted.

questions.prompt: “The portrait is completed by the sparrows rather than by the narrator.” Discuss.
questions.answer: The claim captures how the story allocates its feeling. Throughout the narration the adult grandson withholds emotion: he reports the grandmother’s death in a sentence, does not describe grief, and never states that he loved her, preferring routine and mild comedy to declaration. By the time of the funeral, then, the reader has been given companionship, separation and return, but no expression of loss from the one person positioned to give it. It is at that point that the sparrows arrive, and they do the work the narrator refuses to do. They had been her daily companions in the courtyard for years, so their presence is consistent with her world rather than an intrusion on it; their silence — no chirping, no fluttering — registers a loss more sharply than any described mourning would; and their refusal of bread shows that the loss has removed something essential rather than merely changed the scene. The narrator’s remark that they mourned like us quietly equates the birds with the family, transferring to them the grief he leaves unspoken. There is a second reason the ending completes a portrait: a portrait is defined by its final impression rather than by its biography, and the image of silent sparrows around an old woman’s body summarises her life of devotion and attachment without explanation. The counter-argument is that the narrator has in fact prepared everything: he told us about the sparrows in the city years, so their return is his arrangement, not an accident he observed. That is true, and it strengthens rather than weakens the claim, because arranging evidence while declining to comment is precisely the technique of a portrait — the narrator builds the frame and lets the image speak.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the technique of withheld emotion, the three functions of the sparrows, and a judgement that addresses the objection that the narrator arranged the ending himself.

questions.prompt: The story is comic in its middle and moving at its end. How does the author manage the change of tone?
questions.answer: The management of tone begins with the voice, which is affectionate and self-deprecating from the first page. The humour in the city section is double-edged: the grandmother’s objections to English, science and especially music lessons are presented as bewilderment rather than folly, and the narrator includes himself among those whose seriousness looks small from a distance. Because the comedy is never at her expense alone — he is mocked as much as she is — it builds warmth rather than ridicule, and it establishes a register from which a quiet ending can fall. The change is then prepared by structure rather than announced. The city years already introduce the separation, the five years abroad empty the house of him entirely, and the evening of singing and drums is written as a brief reunion whose very joy implies that it will not last: the reader is being readied for the illness before it is mentioned. When the death comes, the narrator strips the sentence of ceremony — she prayed, she died — and the absence of elaboration is itself the tonal pivot, because after so much understatement the reader supplies the feeling. The sparrows then carry what the narration will not: their silence and their refusal of bread are stated as observation, and the emotional weight accumulates from plain facts rather than from adjectives. The craft lesson the passage offers is therefore that tone is controlled by selection and restraint: establish affection through comedy, remove the shared routine stage by stage, report the death plainly, and let a precise image hold the grief. An examiner awarding marks for style should be shown these stages with a phrase from each, because the movement from humour to pathos in this story is a designed sequence and not a change of subject.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the stages of the tonal movement with textual illustration and the observation that restraint rather than intensity produces the ending’s effect.
